Open thread • Replies: 20 • Updated: 2026-11-27 04:38 UTC

OP

If we continue at the current rate of automation sure companies can create more things for cheaper and lets assume the quality is at least as good, however less people will be needed to create these things. As jobs are lost the money those jobs create AND the consumers those jobs create will also go as people wont have money to purchase products. Surely this is bad for literally everyone no matter how rich they are. Is anyone seriously considering this?

And yet, there is no shortage of people providing bogus claims that attempt to convince others that they do, in fact, understand or comprehend. This is because they, and even you, intuitively understand that an answer alone is not nearly as valuable as the process to obtain an answer. This is more than mere semantics, all answers are necessarily based on incomplete, imperfect, or just plain wrong information. A good answer, one that shows its work, can incorporate small changes to its inputs with small amounts of work. LLMs cannot do this, they must start over from the very beginning, because they cannot "show their work", nor can they understand a process and follow or tweak it as they go, they can only start over from the very beginning, they can just do so at enormous scale, which is the basis of agentic loops. LLMs cannot modify or change how they work on the fly. A human mind can build a model of what it knows, and, in LLM terminology, dynamically compress and decompress its "context" to suite what is important at a given time. An LLM must re-process its entire context every time, or rely on its human operator to lossfully and inelegantly compress previous context. An LLM is incapable of reflecting on its own history and revising its context. These are all things that a human mind can do without even consciously thinking about it, but that LLMs are definitionally incapable of, and they have direct consequences on not just their output, but their ability to sustain their output into the future. Perhaps there is a future, as of yet undiscovered model of computation that can more accurately do these things that could conceivable be called "AI", but LLMs are not it, and will never be it.

Being able to factor integers in polynomial time in theory makes it practical to crack RSA encryption. RSA is public/private key encryption, which is the basis for essentially all of internet traffic. If you can break that, everything you can hoover up from the internet is viewable by you. But, "polynomial time" is still a potentially super expensive thing. If you have n things, and you can process them in n steps, that's polynomial time - linear. If you can process them in n^2 steps, that's also polynomial time, but it becomes super slow very quickly by the size of the input. n^1000 + n^800 + 10n^50 is also polynomial time, and that would be so ridiculous, it wouldn't make a difference. You still couldn't crack things that expensive.

This is such a normie take.

1. Home Depot and Lowes didn’t sell made in USA Craftsman tools. They were hands down the best store brand rivaling PB Swiss or Klein. Like really they were outstanding for the price. They had the shovels where the wood handle was steamed and forced into the curve of the metal head. The quality they once represented was outstanding. Lowes and Home Depot were the cheap stores with made in China crap that broke under half the strain.

So step 1 here is Sears held the position of high quality. They got a bunch of Harvard businessmen to take over who offshored all production to the cheapest manufacturers. That quality disappeared. Home owners and professionals used to be key segments for their shoppers, people who wanted quality. They sold Electrolux and Maytag and had lifetime warranties. And across the board they gave those things up. Then they were competing directly with Lowes and Home Depot when they didn’t need to be. Higher profit margins looked good in the short term but it ultimately lost them their niche and key distinct segments.

2. They had a functional e-commerce website selling tools before Amazon did. Amazon was selling books when you could get new Lawn mower parts express delivered to a job site same day. All the store locations beat Amazon at the time and you might pay for it but if you were a professional and needed a HVAC part that day for a client, they could fucking do it because they had stores and warehouses everywhere. Nobody could touch them.

But their website was shit. They had placeholder images everywhere. They barely hired designers and didnmt hire any user research, and the site just continued to have major problems that they never fixed. Over time Amazon became a giant and rivaled their convenience except Sears languished. Broken images all over the site, annoying popups everywhere, they built it without ever hearing about millers law, Their homepage was always a single giant content slider.

62967666
>>62967618
To sum up point two, they basically had a poorly working bootstrapped site running the same layout for over a decade with creeping issues. The UX was atrocious. Same thing happened to Circuit City. They used exclusively brand colors even though innate human responses see meaning in color. It failed to be accessible. Missing images also meant no alt text. Etc. Their site was also causing errors. You could see and order a brown belt and get a black one. Item numbers and titles didn’t match images. Their site was run by a skelleton crew when it should have been the main focus. The old guard at the company wanted to spend how had always worked, much like blockbuster, the leaders making the website good left and they diverted funding to open more physical locations instead of fix issues. They had this concept of brand loyalty which does not exist on the internet.

3. Their management was so obsessed with lowering costs that they offshored developers before it was cool and that quarter some Harvard MBA got to be credited with making millions and moved on to other jobs. While Sears dot com suddenly couldn’t fix basic issues. But it cost them less to run so the store first VPs loved it.

4. The nail in the coffin was that the bad site stopped being useful for trade workers. Nobody wants to buy and pay for aame day shipping of an HVAC part when there’s no image of it and a part number doesn’t match the title. They would pay money and get the wrong thing just too often. By then Amazon had started selling similar parts and Evay and both had expedited or same day shipping but were more reliable. So they lost the last niche keeping them going.

Websites matter a lot even if your business is historically somewhere else. Do not neglect it.
